info.title: agentes.chat operator API
info.description: Workspace and account lookups, what a run did and why a message started one or none, what a workspace connected, recorded, asked and scheduled, what a person was notified of and reaches, the messages no run answered, the job queue, the emails queued to an address and what model calls spent, the times a member asked for help, one piece of what a workspace wrote read with a reason and a member's support request answered by email (the reveal door), a workspace told afterwards that its content was read to investigate suspected abuse, workspace standing, billing holds and limits (ADR 0079), a workspace's logo and accent color (ADR 0193), the extra hostnames this server answers on with their look (ADR 0194), outside collaborators (ADR 0191), the events feed and review blocks, the workspaces' computers from an external provisioner, who may sign up (the waiting list and early-access invitations, ADR 0078), how new Claude sign-ins for all agents are made (ADR 0150), and how connectors are used (ADR 0103), for the people who run this instance (ADR 0056).

operator.description: This server's `OPERATOR_API_TOKEN`. Or its `OPERATOR_API_READ_TOKEN`, accepted only for `GET` and `HEAD` and never under `/review/`: anything else answers 403 `forbidden`. Under `/reveal/` neither is accepted: only `OPERATOR_API_REVEAL_TOKEN` is, for `POST` alone, and it is refused (403) everywhere else. On a server that didn't set it, every path under `/reveal/` answers 403.

eventLoopLag.description: How late this process ran what was due over its last minute, from the runtime's own sampling (also logged as `event loop lag`). Null: no minute ended yet.

state.description: `off` without both Turnstile keys. While `unreachable` (this server can't reach Cloudflare) or `secret_refused` (Cloudflare refuses `TURNSTILE_SECRET_KEY`), every request goes through unchecked.

blocked.description: Networks refused in the last 10 minutes because their page couldn't load the check (`human_check_blocked`), each counted once: an IPv4 address, or an IPv6 /64. Any client can claim its page couldn't load it, so read it beside `passed`.

passed.description: Tokens Cloudflare passed in the last 10 minutes. When the widget is down for everyone, `blocked` rises while this falls. Clients claiming it is down don't move it.

testing.description: `TURNSTILE_SECRET_KEY` is one of Cloudflare's test secrets. They refuse real tokens, and the one that passes takes a public dummy token from anyone. Right only on a test server.

OperatorStandingNotice.description: `shown`: the workspace is told the reason, the change goes into its audit log and a new state notifies its owners and admins. `silent`: it is told only that it is paused, and nothing is written where it can read it. Use `silent` only when an authority's order forbids telling them.

In a full workspace they read that they can add a seat, and anyone else who manages billing reads to ask them, by name while they are in the workspace. OperatorOutsideAccessState.description: `pending`: a request waits for someone in the workspace who may invite people to approve or deny it. `member`: they are in, as an outside collaborator.

enrollCode.description: Single use. The computer redeems it at `POST /api/machines/device/token` (`{ deviceCode }`) on the public address, like a confirmed connection code. Never log it.

allOf.description: How far the workspace's own computer is, as a provisioner last said; null: nothing said.

managed.description: The workspace's own computer, the one you issue.

standby.description: You put the workspace's computer in standby (`PUT …/standby`) and it hasn't connected since. False for every other computer.

busy.description: The workspace's computer is in use now: a run of the workspace queued or running, a run waiting for this computer, a task running on it, someone in control of one of its agents' screens, or someone wanting it in the last 2 minutes (an open view of it asks every few seconds). Busy in standby: something waits for it. False for every other computer.

lastUsedAt.description: When the workspace's computer was last used: the latest of the workspace's runs and this computer's tasks of the last 7 days, the last time something wanted it, and its people's last visit. Null for every other computer, or when nothing says.

executors.description: What its runner found on it that says its version: its coding CLIs (`claude`, `codex`…) and its agents' `browser`. `version` is the line each printed; null when that isn't a plain version.

statusUnknown.description: Its runner's last look at `status` was inconclusive.

accountCount.description: How many AI accounts it has.

openTasks.description: Background tasks queued or running on it, and interrupted ones that may still come back.

holds.description: What agents keep running on it now (`keep_running`).

waitingRuns.description: Runs waiting for it: for it to come back, or for room on it.

deletedAt.description: When it was removed. Always null in a workspace's list, which leaves removed computers out.

mode.description: `invite`: only people with an invitation sign up (a workspace's, or early access). `open`: anyone. Always `invite` while this server is its agents' computer (`HOST_COMPUTER_TOKEN`).

forcedOpen.description: `ALLOW_SIGNUP=true` on this server: sign-up is open whatever `mode` says.

emails.description: This server sends email, so invitations can go out.

unconfirmed.description: Entries that never confirmed their address.

put.summary: Hold, suspend or restore a workspace
put.description: Enforced by this server where work starts: model calls, computer calls, routines, invitations and, when suspended, every permission check. Suspending also stops its runs and its tasks on computers now; cutting a computer's network is up to the operator's own controls on it. Held or suspended, it waits for no computer: what its provisioner last said goes (a ready computer stays), and it is a request again once active. It takes effect at once in this process and within 5 seconds in the server's others. Setting what is already set tells nobody again.

reason.description: Shown to the workspace with the notice `shown`, its owners' notice included. On agentes.chat Cloud, `review` reads as the automatic review hold's line, `review.<category>` as that line naming what was flagged (`phishing_impersonation`, `account_takeover`, `fraud` or `illegal_content`, any other category reading as plain `review`), `ended` (a plan that ended) as it is, and any other reason is followed by how to contest it, so name the Terms section it rests on.

put.summary: Hold one agent, or let it go
put.description: Held, the agent starts nothing (no run, model call, computer work, routine or bridge call) and is never picked to answer; the rest of the workspace works. What it is doing stops at its next model, computer or bridge call. The workspace reads only that the agent is paused, never the reason. On agentes.chat Cloud it reads the hold's kind with how to contest it (`network` for a reason starting with `network.`, else `operator`), and the agent's responsible person and the workspace's owners and admins get a notice, replaced when it is held again for another kind and closed when the agent is let go. At once in this process, within 5 seconds in the others.

put.summary: Hold a workspace's deletion (a legal hold), or let it go
put.description: While held, a workspace whose deletion was asked for (by an owner, or with its only member's account) waits past its date instead of being deleted: it stays closed, with everything in it. Nothing is refused and the workspace is told nothing: no audit row, no notice. Restoring the workspace never lifts it. Let go, a deletion past its date goes ahead within an hour.

put.summary: Block an account, or let it back
put.description: Blocked: its sessions and phones are signed out now, it can't sign in again, every workspace refuses it on its next request (no waiting for a session cookie to expire) and its open connections close. Unblocking lets it sign in again; it keeps its workspaces. On agentes.chat Cloud the refused sign-in reads the block's kind, never its reason: `abuse` for `abuse.resignup`, `legal` for `legal_hold`, else `other`.

put.summary: Put a billing hold on a workspace, change its code, or lift it
put.description: A billing hold is a hold with one of these codes as its reason and the notice `shown`: the workspace reads it in its own words, and owners and admins get the way to fix it. It never replaces nor lifts a hold set through PUT /standing or a suspension (`applied: false`); one of those replaces it, so set it again once that is lifted. Its owners and admins are notified when the state changes.

All at once. Enforced where each is used: joining and inviting (`org.members_full`), every file written to this server's storage (`storage.full`, `storage.daily_full`), the platform's AI (within a minute). Lowering one takes nothing away: people stay, files stay, only what is new is refused. Allowed whatever the workspace's standing. Setting what is already set changes nothing, `updatedAt` included.

post.summary: Ask a workspace to let an account in as an outside collaborator
post.description: Files a request to join that whoever may invite people in the workspace approves or denies like any other, told the same way. Approved, the account joins at once and never counts toward the `members` limit, even in a full workspace. Asking again while the request waits changes nothing. 409 `join.member` when the account is already in the workspace, `join.waiting` while another request to join waits for its address, `join.full` while 50 outside requests already wait in the workspace (counted apart from the asks through its invitation links), `outside_access.account_closed` when the account is blocked or waiting for its deletion (one that becomes so while its request waits has the request closed when someone approves it, with `outside_access.ended`). The events feed tells the answer: `outside_access.granted` or `outside_access.denied`, and `outside_access.ended` when they leave or are removed, or when the request is over unanswered (run out, told by a daily sweep, or gone with the account), each with `data.userId`.

put.summary: Say how far the workspace's computer is
put.description: Its people see it live, with the time left and the stage. The time `since` restarts only when the state, step or reason change. One wait counts down to the earliest ready time you gave it: a later one changes nothing they see, so a part running long reads as running over, until another state, a removal or a hold starts a new wait. A ready time over a minute ahead (the wait's earliest), `waiting` or `problem` tells the owners they'll get an email when it's ready (when this server sends email). Refused (409 `provisioning.ready`) once the computer is ready, until it is removed, and (403 `org.paused`, `org.suspended`, `org.deleting`) unless the workspace is active and not being deleted: one held, suspended or being deleted waits for no computer, and what you last said of it is gone.

state.description: `ready` is not yours to set: it comes with the computer's first hello.

step.description: With `preparing`: reserving, starting, installing or connecting; ignored otherwise.

stage.description: With `preparing`: what the computer is doing within `step` (ordering, wiping, starting, booting, updating, restarting, network, firewall, apps, connecting); ignored otherwise. Any word is kept: the apps say one they have no words for as its step.

reason.description: With `waiting`: capacity; ignored otherwise. `approval`, from an older client, reads as capacity.

expectedReadyAt.description: With `preparing`: when the computer should be ready, at most 7 days ahead; ignored otherwise. A wait counts down to the earliest time it was told: a later one, or a report without one, leaves it as it is, so people see the wait run over.

The code lives 10 minutes; once redeemed, the computer's first hello makes it ready and gives it the workspace's agents that have no computer. Refused (403 `org.paused`, `org.suspended`, `org.deleting`) unless the workspace is active and not being deleted.

put.summary: Say the workspace's computer is in standby, or no longer
put.description: Say it when you put the computer to sleep (`true`), or that it no longer is (`false`; its first hello clears it too). In standby nothing is wrong to its people: it opens as it wakes, and it is never listed as disconnected. Whatever wants it meanwhile (a run, a person opening it, a request to it) records `machine.wake_wanted` in the events feed, at most every 10 seconds per computer: wake it then. A run waits up to a minute for it before it tells its people the computer isn't answering. `true` again keeps the first time it was said. 404 when the workspace has no such managed computer.

Its people see a line saying so on the computer, never an error, while it is online. `true` again keeps the first time it was said; removing the computer ends it. A change comes as `machine.updated`. 404 when the workspace has no such managed computer.

post.summary: Invite addresses to create an account and make workspaces

An address that has an account gets no link: the account is allowed at once, and an email in its language says so (none to a blocked account). An allowed account makes workspaces once its address is confirmed. One invitation per address: inviting it again sends the same invitation a new link (the old one stops working), unless `resend` is false. Answers come in the request's order, once per address. Outcomes: `invalid_email`, `signed_up` (its invitation made an account or allowed one already, so nothing went out), `allowed`, `already_invited` (with `resend: false`), `recent` (sent in the last 2 minutes, so nothing went out), `resent`, `invited`. post.summary: Read one field of one record of what a workspace wrote, with a reason
post.description: Only with `OPERATOR_API_REVEAL_TOKEN`. One record a call, at most 2000 characters, for one of three purposes. Two are proved by a record of the workspace. For `member_request`: the support request is this workspace's and recent (403 `reveal.no_request`), its member still is one (`reveal.requester`) and reads the record in the app now (`reveal.not_visible`). For `fault`: the run failed or got stuck in its days (`reveal.no_fault`), the record is its step, the message that started it or one it wrote, its agent's instructions, its routine or a task it started, or, for a run that went on past a failed step, that step's `error` and its call's `input` alone (`reveal.not_the_fault`), and it is not of a direct conversation (`reveal.direct_conversation`). For `trust_safety`, a safety review to investigate suspected abuse, no record proves the purpose and the call names none (`requestId` or `runId` with it is a 400): this server has no record of an abuse investigation, so your own service answers for the cause. It opens every kind but a support request's words (`reveal.not_visible`), and of a direct conversation never a message that no agent wrote and that started no run (`reveal.direct_conversation`). What a run of a confidential thread holds opens under no purpose: its steps and a task it started answer 403 `reveal.confidential` where the purpose would have opened them, and a message of such a thread reads as its stub. Before any text is read, the read is recorded: a `content.viewed` event with the reason, and, for `member_request` and `fault`, an entry in the workspace's own audit log (`operator.content_read`) with what was read, the purpose and its proof, never the reason. A read for `trust_safety` writes the event and no entry: you tell the workspace afterwards with `POST /orgs/{orgId}/content-reads/disclosure`, when your review ends and 7 days after the read at the latest. A record of another workspace, a deleted one and one nobody has answer the same 404. An `error` of something that did not fail is 409 `reveal.no_error`. At most 30 calls a minute (429 `reveal.limit_minute`), 100 reads of one workspace in 24 hours (`reveal.limit_workspace`) and, on the whole server, 150 reads for `trust_safety` in 24 hours (`reveal.limit_untold`).

404.description: No such record in this workspace

post.summary: Answer a member's support request at the address of their account
post.description: Only with `OPERATOR_API_REVEAL_TOKEN`. An email to the address the request's account has now, in that account's language: one of this server's own sentences (`template`) or your own words (`text`, plain text of at most 2000 characters). No argument names an address, a name or a subject. The email says that this server answers, that an AI assistant wrote it when `assistedByAi`, and where to write back when `SUPPORT_EMAIL` is set. A reply reads nothing: a request can be answered after the 30 days in which it opens content, for the 90 days its words are kept (403 `reveal.request_old` after that). Its member must still be one (`reveal.requester`). A request of another workspace and one nobody has answer the same 404. In one transaction with the email's job, the reply is recorded: a `support.replied` event and an entry in the workspace's own audit log (`operator.support_replied`), each with the request, the template or the word `text`, how long your words were and `assistedByAi`. Never the words: they are in the email's job alone, and leave it once the email is sent or given up. At most 3 replies to one request (429 `reveal.limit_request`) and 60 from this server in 24 hours (`reveal.limit_day`), counted from those events; a call counts toward the door's 30 a minute (`reveal.limit_minute`). A server that sends no email answers 409 `reveal.no_email`.

400.description: Invalid request: both or neither of `template` and `text`, or a `text` that says nothing

post.summary: Tell a workspace, afterwards, that its content was read to investigate suspected abuse
post.description: Only with `OPERATOR_API_TOKEN`. An operator that read content for `trust_safety` tells the workspace afterwards that it did: one entry in the workspace's own audit log (`operator.content_review_disclosed`, actor `system`) with the period and how many items, and nothing else: no reason, no record, no text. You owe it when your review ends, and 7 days after the read at the latest. The same `from` and `to` again answer the entry first written and write nothing, so a call that timed out can be sent again; another period writes its own entry.

400.description: Invalid request: a period that has not ended, is backwards or too long, or a count out of bounds

put.summary: Register a hostname, or replace its look (ADR 0194)
put.description: On that host the pages before sign-in show its name, logo and accent, and sign-in is by email alone. Point the hostname at this server and serve a certificate for it first: the server only answers what reaches it. It runs no bot check, and nothing ties an account to a host, so any account's email lookup, password sign-in and reset can be asked there: what guards them is the limits per network, tighter on registered hosts (10 email lookups in 10 minutes and 5 sign-ups in 15 minutes per network, for all of them together), and the wrong passwords per account (10 in 15 minutes from one network, 50 from all), each counted in a server process's memory, so a restart starts them again (ADR 0075). Applies at once on this process and within 30 s on the others. Refusals: `host.invalid` (not a hostname: no scheme, port or path, at least one dot), `host.own` (`PUBLIC_URL`'s host or one of `EXTRA_TRUSTED_ORIGINS`), `host.too_many` (409, past 1000), `host.needs_https` (409, `PUBLIC_URL` isn't https, so the session cookies a registered host sets would carry no Secure flag), and a logo's as for a workspace's (`logo.type`, `logo.too_large`, `logo.not_base64`, `logo.empty`).
